rationale: B wins by a nose because it keeps the caveats closer to the sell: "Without at least one number, this collapses into speculation" is the line a founder actually needs before walking into the business-model angle. A has the sharper publisher headline, "Perplexity will pay publishers it cites. It won't say how much," but it also gets loose with "the company's first structural answer" and "first concrete monetization signal since the raise." Both are strong; B just does slightly less decorating of the holes.
gaps_in_A: "This is the company's first structural answer to that fight" is an unsupported first. The update says the program launches now, not that Perplexity has never offered another answer before.
"takes a referral fee on every sale" overstates the fact. The update says Perplexity earns a referral fee from in-app purchases, not that every sale or recommendation carries one.

"The launch is the first concrete monetization signal since the raise" invents sequence and exclusivity. The facts give a recent multi-billion valuation, not a clean before-and-after investor narrative.
"Merchants deciding whether to list will want the terms this week" assumes a merchant-listing workflow the update never gives you.
gaps_in_B: "after months of legal threats" invents duration. The update says Perplexity has faced criticism and legal threats; it does not say months.

"the company accused of taking publisher content is now proposing to pay for it" is punchy, but it compresses criticism and legal threats into a specific accusation. Fine as a reporting frame only if sourced elsewhere.
"trade commerce press cheering the launch" is lazy audience psychology. Name the beat and incentive, not the imaginary mood of the reporter.

The commerce proof list asks for "which merchants and product categories are live" and fee structure, but misses two obvious retailer questions A caught better: paid placement and who handles purchase/returns.
